newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Amcor to fix U.S./German operations.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Amcor to fix U.S./German operations.

text.p: Amcor Ltd managing director Don Macfarlane said on Friday the paper and packaging company would concentrate on reducing costs and reviving struggling operations in Germany and the United States in 1996/97.

Macfarlane said the company believed the current financial year would be a difficult one, and the Melbourne-based bluechip firm needed to focus on internal efficiencies to save money and improve its performance. "We have done A$50 million a year (in cost reductions) for the last three years and we would like to be approaching something that was nearly double that," he said.

He also told reporters after the annual general meeting in Sydney that Amcor would slash capital expenditure this year to about A$500 million from more than A$800 million last year, reflecting the wind-back of its acquistion strategy.
Earlier, he told shareholders the German fibre packaging operation, Holfelder, was facing radical change but at best would only go close to break even this year.

"In terms of underperforming businesses, probably our most troublesome one has been Holfelder in Germany," he said, adding that the U.S.-based Cello Bag packaging and McKinley Paper operations would also face radical overhauls.
Amcor aimed to either return Cello Bag and McKinley Paper back to profitability, or reorganise and rationalise these units which could involve winding them into joint ventures.

Cello Bag lost a major customer in 1995/96 which affected its profit contribution while McKinley Paper, a paperboard division with 150,000 tonnes of annual capacity, is competing in an over-supplied market.
These operations will receive very similar treatment to that now underway in Germany, specifically a management overhaul and the use of industry experts to advise on restructuring, Macfarlane said.
In its 1995/96 annual report, Amcor blamed the weak Germany economy for most of Holfelder's woes and said it had appointed a new chief executive for the operation in August this year.
"I would see Holfelder profitable, but not hugely, in 1997/98," Macfarlane told reporters. He said the U.S. operations were under the microscope but would not be offloaded.
"One might try to joint venture them, roll them into soemthing else, manage them a different way," he said.
"There's a lot of options but I can't imagine that we would be closing them."

Investors, who have faced a weaker share price since Amcor early last month reported its first annual profit fall in more than 10 years, were told by chairman Athol Lapthorne that the first six months of 1996/97 also looked bad.
Net profit in 1995/96 fell six percent to A$338.8 million.
Results in the final half year to June 30, 1997 could be somewhat stronger, he said.
Macfarlane said the full year would be "very tough unless something amazing happens in the second half of the year".
